extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examination on how to determine and apply prior art dates under 35 U.S.C. 102 (including subsections (a),(b),(c),(d),(e)) and how to overcome related rejections. Covers rules for U.S. patents, U.S. application publications, WIPO/PCT publications, benefit/priority claims, and examiner procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(e) inventive-entity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to apply a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), the inventive entity of the application must be different than that of the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there are joint inventors, only one inventor needs to be different for the inventive entities to be different and a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) is applicable even if there are some inventors in common between the application and the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised 35 U.S.C. 102(e) applicability and retroactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (AIPA and later amendments) applies in the examination of all applications, whenever filed, and the reexamination of, or other proceedings to contest, all patents; the filing date of the application being examined is no longer relevant in determining what version of 35 U.S.C. 102(e) to apply, with a single exception for certain international applications filed prior to November 29, 2000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The revised statutory provisions supersede previous versions of 35 U.S.C. 102(e) and 374 except when the potential reference is based on an international application filed prior to November 29, 2000. The provisions amending 102(e) and 374 in Pub. L. 107-273 are completely retroactive to the effective date of the AIPA (November 29, 2000). See MPEP § 706.02(f)(1) for examination guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of references that may be applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential reference must be a U.S. patent, a U.S. application publication (35 U.S.C. 122(b)) or a WIPO publication of an international application under PCT Article 21(2) in order to apply the reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reference did not result from or claim the benefit of an international application, its 102(e) date is the earliest effective U.S. filing date, taking into consideration any proper benefit claims under 119(e) or 120 if the prior application(s) properly supports the subject matter used to make the rejection in compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-condition test for treating an international filing date as a U.S. filing date under 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: An international filing date is a U.S. filing date for 102(e) prior art purposes only if (a) the international application has an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000; (b) it designated the United States; and (c) it was published under PCT Article 21(2) in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all three conditions are met, the international filing date is the 102(e) prior art date. If the international application properly claims benefit to an earlier-filed U.S. or international application (or provisional), and the earlier application properly supports the subject matter per 35 U.S.C. 112, the earlier filing date may be the effective prior art date.

rubrics_metrics.name: International application filed on/after Nov 29, 2000 but not designating US or not published in English
rubrics_metrics.description: If the international application was filed on or after November 29, 2000 but did not designate the United States or was not published in English under PCT Article 21(2), do not treat the international filing date as a U.S. filing date for prior art purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this situation, do not apply the reference as of its international filing date or as of completion of 371(c) requirements. The reference may be applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b) as of its publication date, or under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as of any later U.S. filing date of an application that properly claimed the benefit of the international application (if applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: International applications filed prior to Nov 29, 2000 (pre-AIPA treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: International applications filed prior to November 29, 2000 are subject to the former (pre-AIPA) version of 35 U.S.C. 102(e) and 374; WIPO and U.S. publications of such IAs do not have a 102(e) date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For U.S. patents issued from such an international application, apply 102(e) as of the earlier of the date of completion of 371(c)(1),(2) and (4) or the filing date of the later-filed U.S. continuing application that claimed the benefit. Application publications based on pre-November 29, 2000 IAs are prior art only under 102(a) or (b) as of their publication dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for references that claim benefit/priority
rubrics_metrics.description: The 102(e) date of a reference that claims benefit under 119(e) (provisional) or 120 (earlier U.S. nonprovisional) is the earliest effective U.S. filing date to which proper benefit is claimed, provided the earlier application properly supports the subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider whether benefit/priority claims are properly perfected (e.g., certified priority documents filed, English translations if necessary) and whether the earlier application enables and describes the subject matter used to make the rejection (see 37 CFR 1.55 and 1.78 requirements and MPEP §§ 201.11, 201.13, 706.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a) applicability and considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: For 35 U.S.C. 102(a) to apply, the reference must have a publication date earlier in time than the effective filing date of the application, and must not be applicant’s own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a reference is prior art under 102(e), the examiner should still consider 102(a) because the corresponding WIPO publication or international application under PCT Article 21(2) may be the earliest prior art date under 102(a). Also, references only prior art under 102(e)/(f)/(g) and used in a 103(a) rejection may be disqualified under 103(c) if commonly owned at the time the invention was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(b) can be overcome by: (A) persuasively arguing claims are patentably distinguishable; (B) amending claims to be patentably distinguishable; (C) perfecting benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78(a) (including amending the specification or filing an ADS) and establishing that the prior application satisfies 35 U.S.C. 112(first paragraph); or (D) perfecting benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) by complying with 37 CFR 1.78(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a benefit claim is perfected, the rejection must be reconsidered to determine whether the prior art still qualifies as 102(b) or now qualifies under 102(a). See MPEP §§ 201.11 and 706.02 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e) can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentable distinctions; (B) amending claims; (C) filing an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the reference invention is not by 'another'; (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing prior invention (with limitations); (E) submitting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) in time or filing a grantable petition under 37 CFR 1.55(c); or (F) perfecting benefit under 119(e) or 120 within the time periods set in 37 CFR 1.78(a) or filing a grantable petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 1.131 affidavit is not acceptable if the claims of the reference and the application are directed to the same invention or are obvious variants. If there is a common assignee or inventor between the application and patent, a double patenting rejection must be made. If there is no common assignee/inventor and 102(e) is the only possible rejection, the examiner must determine whether an interference should be declared. See MPEP § 715, § 716.10, § 804, and Chapter 2300.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(a) can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentable distinctions; (B) amending claims; (C) filing a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit showing prior invention (if the reference is not a U.S. patent or U.S. app publication claiming the same patentable invention); (D) filing a 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit showing reference invention is not by 'another'; (E) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); or (F) perfecting benefit under 119(e) or 120.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 1.131 affidavit is inappropriate when the claims of the reference and the application are directed to the same invention or are obvious variants. See MPEP § 715 for 1.131 requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) vs 102(b) for public use or on-sale knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: If the evidence points to knowledge or a sale occurring within the year prior to the effective filing date, 35 U.S.C. 102(a) applies; if the activity occurred more than one year prior to the effective filing date, 35 U.S.C. 102(b) is applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'in this country' means in the United States only. No rejection under 102(a) should be made if there is evidence that applicant made the invention and only disclosed it to others within the year prior to the effective filing date. See MPEP § 2133.03 for case law on 'public use' and 'on sale' bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for information when public use or on-sale issue is raised (Form Paragraph 7.104)
rubrics_metrics.description: When public use or on-sale activity is raised, the examiner may issue a requirement for additional information necessary to consider patentability under 35 U.S.C. 102(b); the applicant is reminded that failure to fully reply will result in abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner Note: (1) Information sought should be restricted to that reasonably necessary to render a decision (see MPEP § 2133.03). (2) A one- or two-month time period should be set for reply (or SSP time period if part of an Office action with shortened statutory period). (3) If sufficient evidence already exists to establish a prima facie case of public use or on sale, use form paragraph 7.16 to make a 102(b) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(d) statutory-bar four requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 102(d) establishes a statutory bar if all four conditions are present: (A) the foreign application must be filed more than 12 months before the effective filing date of the U.S. application; (B) the foreign and U.S. applications must be filed by the same applicant, legal representatives or assigns; (C) the foreign application must have actually issued as a patent or inventor’s certificate before the filing in the U.S.; and (D) the same invention must be involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such a foreign patent is discovered by the examiner, the rejection is made under 35 U.S.C. 102(d) on the ground of statutory bar. See MPEP § 2135.01 for case law further clarifying each requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search guidance for 35 U.S.C. 102(d) prior art (when to search)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should only undertake a search for an issued foreign patent for use as 102(d) prior art if there is a reasonable possibility that a foreign patent covering the same subject matter has been granted to the same inventive entity before the U.S. effective filing date (i.e., the time between foreign and U.S. filings is greater than the usual time it takes for a patent to issue in the foreign country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normally the probability is slight and such searches may be unproductive, but average pendency varies greatly between foreign countries (examples: in Belgium a patent may be granted in just a month; in Japan it may take several years). The search can be accomplished on an electronic database by the examiner or the Scientific and Technical Information Center staff. See MPEP § 901.06(a) paragraph IV.B for online searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure I — overall flow to determine 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date
rubrics_metrics.description: I. Determine the appropriate 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for each potential reference by following the guidelines and flow charts: (A) confirm reference type (U.S. patent, U.S. app publication, or WIPO publication under PCT Art 21(2)); (B) determine if reference resulted from or claimed benefit of an international application; (C) if so, apply the three-condition test for treating the IA filing date as a U.S. filing date; (D) treat foreign priority/further rules accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reference did not result from nor claim the benefit of an international application, its 102(e) date is its earliest effective U.S. filing date, considering proper benefit claims under 119(e) or 120 and compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. See MPEP § 2136.02 for support considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating common 102(e) factual situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Nine examples (Examples 1–9) illustrate common factual situations (only the most common) for determining the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of references: Example 1: 111(a) application with no priority/benefit claims; Example 2: 111(a) with benefit claim to prior U.S.; Example 3: 111(a) with 119(a)-(d) priority to a foreign application; Examples 4–9 involve international applications and national stage issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples specify that for 111(a) applications with no benefit claims the 102(e) prior art date is the application's actual filing date; for benefit claims the earlier effective U.S. filing date is accorded assuming proper support; and various permutations with IAs depend on filing dates, designation, publication language, and whether the IA is pre- or post-November 29, 2000.
